project: Income Classification using Logistic Regression (UCI Adult Dataset)
author_note: Structured JSON document covering limitations, good-fit criteria, and an end-to-end implementation checklist.

limitations.detail: Logistic regression assumes a linear relationship between the logit of the outcome and the predictors. Real-world income determinants (e.g. interactions between education and occupation) may be highly nonlinear, leading to underfitting.
limitations.mitigation: Engineer interaction/ polynomial terms; compare against tree-based models (Random Forest, GBM).

limitations.detail: Unlike tree-based models, logistic regression does not discover feature interactions unless they are manually specified.

The Adult dataset is from the 1994 U.S. Census. Demographic patterns, income distributions, and the relevance of features like 'fnlwgt' have shifted significantly. Race categories are reductive and U.S.-centric.
limitations.mitigation: Use contemporary equivalents (e.g. ACS data); document ethical considerations prominently.

limitations.detail: Rows with unknown workclass, occupation, or native-country are either dropped or imputed, introducing potential bias.
limitations.mitigation: Compare results with and without missing-value rows; use model-based imputation.

limitations.detail: Race and sex are used as predictor variables. Even with dummy encoding, the model quantifies income disparity along demographic lines. Deploying such a model in hiring, lending, or benefits decisions raises fairness and legal (Equal Credit Opportunity Act, GDPR) concerns.
limitations.mitigation: Remove protected classes from production models; conduct fairness audits (demographic parity, equalised odds); consult legal/compliance teams.

limitations.detail: Even without explicit sensitive attributes, proxy variables (zip code, education level) can reconstruct protected characteristics, perpetuating historical bias.
limitations.mitigation: Test for proxy discrimination; use fairness constraints or adversarial debiasing.

limitations.detail: The minority class is underrepresented. Default accuracy will be misleadingly high (~76% by always predicting '<=50K').
limitations.mitigation: Use stratified splitting, class_weight='balanced', SMOTE, or threshold tuning.

limitations.detail: One-hot encoded categorical features can be collinear if drop_first is not used, inflating coefficient variance.
limitations.mitigation: Always use drop_first=True; check VIF; prefer L2 or ElasticNet if collinearity persists.

limitations.detail: One split gives a point estimate of performance with high variance. The reported metrics may not generalise.
limitations.mitigation: Use k-fold cross-validation; report confidence intervals via bootstrap.

limitations.item: Coefficients only comparable when features are scaled
limitations.detail: With unscaled features, magnitude of coefficients reflects feature scale, not importance. The base project does not scale before fitting.
limitations.mitigation: Apply StandardScaler within a Pipeline; report odds ratios with scaled features.

when_good_fit.rationale: Stakeholders (regulators, auditors, clinicians) need to understand exactly how each feature contributes to predictions. Logistic regression provides transparent, auditable coefficients.
Fast to train and serves as a strong baseline before investing in more complex models. If logistic regression performs well, the added complexity of GBMs/neural networks may not be justified.
With hundreds (not millions) of features and tens of thousands of rows, logistic regression trains quickly and generalises well.
Designed natively for binary outcomes; extends cleanly to multinomial via softmax.
Well-regularised logistic regression produces probability estimates close to true frequencies (good calibration), unlike tree ensembles that often need Platt scaling.
In credit scoring, healthcare, or insurance, the transparency of logistic regression satisfies model governance requirements (e.g. SR 11-7 in U.S. banking).
L1-regularised logistic regression zeroes out irrelevant features, yielding a sparse, interpretable model.

when_not_good_fit.rationale: If decision boundaries are complex (image data, text, intricate interactions), gradient boosting or neural networks will substantially outperform logistic regression.

when_not_good_fit.scenario: Very high-dimensional sparse data (e.g. NLP bag-of-words with 100k+ features)
when_not_good_fit.rationale: Although L1 helps, specialised linear models (e.g. SGDClassifier with hinge loss, LinearSVC) or embedding-based approaches are more efficient.

when_not_good_fit.scenario: Imbalanced data with extreme skew (<1% minority)
when_not_good_fit.rationale: Logistic regression struggles to learn meaningful decision boundaries. Anomaly detection or specialised resampling frameworks are more appropriate.

when_not_good_fit.scenario: Small sample sizes with many predictors (EPV < 10)
when_not_good_fit.rationale: Overfitting risk is high; ridge regression or Bayesian approaches with informative priors are preferable.

phase_1_data_loading_and_inspection: Load data with correct column names (no header in adult.data)
Strip whitespace from all string/object columns
Replace '?' with NaN and audit missing values
Check income class balance with value_counts(normalize=True)
phase_2_eda: Plot univariate distributions (histograms, count plots) for all features
Plot bivariate relationships (boxplots, grouped bar charts) segmented by income
Examine correlation heatmap of numeric features
Identify outliers and skewed distributions (capital-gain, capital-loss)
Document any ethically sensitive features (race, sex, native-country)
phase_3_feature_engineering: Create dummy variables with drop_first=True for nominal categoricals
Consider log-transformation for skewed continuous features
Create interaction terms based on domain knowledge
Decide on binning strategy for age and hours-per-week (optional)
phase_4_preprocessing: Build ColumnTransformer with StandardScaler for numerics, OneHotEncoder for categoricals
Wrap in sklearn Pipeline to prevent data leakage
Set handle_unknown='ignore' in OneHotEncoder for unseen categories at inference
phase_5_model_training: Instantiate LogisticRegression with chosen penalty, C, solver
If using L1 penalty, ensure solver='liblinear' or 'saga'
Set max_iter ≥ 1000 to avoid convergence warnings
phase_6_evaluation: Print classification_report(y_test, y_pred) for precision, recall, F1
Plot ROC curve with diagonal reference line
Report accuracy with caveat if classes are imbalanced
phase_7_interpretation: Create DataFrame mapping feature names to coefficients
Sort and visualise as horizontal bar plot
If features are scaled, rank features by absolute coefficient magnitude
Document which features increase/decrease odds of >50K income
phase_8_validation_and_robustness: Try 3+ values of C and compare (e.g. 0.01, 0.1, 1.0)
Test with class_weight='balanced' and compare recall/F1
phase_9_comparison: Train a Random Forest with similar features
Compare accuracy, F1, ROC-AUC across all three
phase_10_ethical_and_deployment: Conduct fairness audit: compare error rates across demographic groups
Document which sensitive attributes are included/excluded and why
If deploying: save pipeline with joblib/pickle
Write model card: intended use, limitations, performance by subgroup
Set up monitoring for data drift and performance degradation
Ensure reproducibility: pin random_state, record library versions

known_issues: Sensitive attributes (race, sex) included as features
Data from 1994 — may not reflect current patterns
No scaling applied in base project
recommended_extensions: Tune decision threshold based on business cost
